Context type Example sentence Emoticon options

general positive "The weather seems nice today" :) (: ;) :p :D XD ^_^ very positive or joyful "That's fantastic news" :) ;) :p :D XD :3 ^_^ general negative "The movie wasn't very good" :( ): :'( :| :/ >:( >_< very negative or angry "That's bloody stupid" :( :'( :| :/ >:( D: >_< sarcastic "Well that was sensible" :p ;) ;p :/ ... -_-¬_¬

The sets of emoticons presented to participants were taken from a study by Thompson and Filik (2016). The emoticons were selected based on being the most frequently produced in each context of the original study As such, all emoticons used in the present study are all frequently occuring in the relevant context, however we did not subsequently control for individual degree of familiarity.

Each option was presented as an image of 230 × 230 pixels, with the emoticon in the centre in bold Calibri typeface. To avoid order effects, the arrangement of the seven emoticons was randomised for each participant, with 'other' always being the eighth option.

Section 2 -Contextual Suitability

The second section prompted ratings of suitability for emoticons in the same five types of context used in the first section. The same illustrative sentences were also repeated. Here, instead of a grid of all options, participants were presented with one emoticon at a time and asked to rate its suitability for the given context type. Ratings were given on a 7-point scale, with poles labelled 'very unsuitable' and 'very suitable'.

For each context, an intentionally unsuitable emoticon was included. This was intended to encourage participant attention during the task, and could be used as an exclusion criterion if required. If all emoticon options were at least somewhat suitable to the context, participants might pay less attention to their judgements, whereas the inclusion of unsuitable emoticons requires participants to more closely consider their ratings. The unsuitable options were taken from the same production study as above (Thompson & Filik, 2016); for this purpose, we selected emoticons that had never produced in the given context, but were still commonly used in other contexts.

Table 2. List of context types and the emoticons that were each rated for suitability in the given context. The final emoticon in each set is intentionally unsuitable. Context type Emoticons general positive :) (: ;) :p :D XD ^_^ [>:( very positive or joyful :) ;) :p :D XD :3 ^_^ [:'( general negative :( ): :'( :| :/ >:( >_< :D very negative or angry :( :'( :| :/ >:( D: >_< [^_^ sarcastic :p ;) ;p :/ ... -_-¬_¬ :O Section 3 -Meaning Equivalence

The third section examined meaning equivalence between emoticons. Participants were presented with an array of emoticons along with a reference emoticon. Their task was to select any emoticons they judged as having the same meaning as the given reference emoticon. Participants could alternatively select 'none'. As before, we chose emoticons that were used with high frequency in positive, negative, and sarcastic messages in Thompson and Filik's (2016) production study, with the most frequently used emoticons serving as our reference emoticons.

Final section -Additional Information

A final section asked demographic information, such as age, gender identity, and native language, as well as which messaging apps participants frequently used, and how often they used emoticons in their messages.

Procedure

The study was run online using the Typeform survey platform and could be completed on any computer, phone, or tablet with internet access. Following the ethics statement, participants moved through the sections outlined above. Selections and ratings were given by either clicking or tapping the appropriate response. Trials were presented in a set order, though the array of options provided within each trial were displayed in a random order. An example of a 'selection' type trial is given in Figure 1. At the end of the study there was an option to leave an email address for entry into the prize draw. The study typically took around 10 minutes to complete.

Results

All data were analysed in R (version 4.3.3; R Core Team, 2024). Binary data (usage and meaning equivalence) were analysed using generalised linear mixed-effects models with the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) and ordinal data (suitability) were analysed using cumulative link mixed models with the ordinal package (Christensen, 2023). In each analysis, participant response was modelled as a function of the fixed effects of native language and emoticon. Native language had two levels (L1 vs L2); emoticon had seven levels, with the set of seven emoticons being specific to each context type. Holm-adjustment was used to correct for multiple comparisons within each model. Random intercepts for participants were included in all models. Model outcomes and pairwise comparisons were calculated using the emmeans package (Lenth, 2018). We report mean probability estimates, Odds Ratios (OR), 95% Confidence Intervals (CIs), and Holm-adjusted p-values.

Emoticon Use

The overall likelihood of emoticon use across the various contexts was the same for L1 (mean: 0.19) and L2 (0.19) users of English (OR = 1.03, 95% CI [0.85;1.24], p = .787). Both groups were most likely to use an emoticon in the general positive context (L1: 0.38 and L2: 0.37), followed by general negative contexts (0.31 and 0.27, respectively), then very positive contexts (0.32 and 0.26), and sarcastic contexts (both groups at 0.22), finally being least likely to use emoticons in very negative contexts (0.20 and 0.21).

The probabilities of L1 and L2 English participants using each individual emoticon in either a general positive context or very positive context are given in Figure 2, presented in descending order of overall likelihood of use.

Figure 3 presents the same for general negative contexts and very negative contexts, and Figure 4 presents this data for sarcastic contexts. See Appendix Table A1 for full model outputs. groups. Following Holm adjustments for multiple comparisons, only two emoticons differed significantly between groups. The :p emoticon was more likely to be used by the L1 English group (0.33) than the L2 group (0.17) (OR = 2.44, 95% CI [1.27;4.71], p = .047). Conversely, the ^_^ emoticon was more likely to be used by the L2 English group (0.19) than the L1 group (0.05) (OR = 0.21, 95% CI [0.09;0.49], p = .002). For all other emoticons, there were no significant differences between L1 and L2 (all ps > .1).

For very positive contexts, L1 and L2 participants again agreed on the emoticons they were most likely to use, which in this instance were the :D and :) emoticons. The only emoticon to show a significant difference was ^_^ (OR = 0.30, 95% CI [0.14;0.66], p = .019), with L2 participants more likely to use it (0.18) than L1s (0.06). All other ps > .5. In general negative, very negative, and sarcastic contexts, L1 and L2 groups did not significantly differ in their likelihood of use for any of the emoticons. All ps > .1.

Descriptively, in general negative contexts, the two groups agreed on the two most likely emoticons, while agreement was a little less clear for very negative contexts, and showed least agreement in the sarcastic contexts.

For all kaomoji (right-way up emoticons), L2 users of English were consistently more likely to use them than L1s: significantly so in the case of the ^_^ emoticon, and descriptively in the case of the >_< and -_and ¬_¬ emoticons.

Contextual Suitability

For each of the following contexts, the intentionally unsuitable emoticon was consistently rated as highly unsuitable, confirming that participants were using the scale appropriately.

The intentionally unsuitable emoticons are excluded from the figures and analyses. In the following results, a positive rating indicates suitability for the given context, negative ratings indicate an emoticon is unsuited, and a rating close to zero indicates the emoticon is seen as neither particularly suitable nor particularly unsuitable.

The suitability ratings from L1 and L2 participants for each individual emoticon in general positive contexts and very positive contexts are given in Figure 5, arranged in Emoticon variation and meaning descending order of overall rating. Figure 6 gives the same for general negative contexts and very negative contexts, and Figure 7 gives the data for sarcastic contexts. See Appendix Table A2 for full model outputs. The wink face ;) emoticon was rated as significantly more suitable by L2s than by L1s for both general positive (0.47 vs -0.5; OR = 0.28, 95% CI [0.17;0.47], p < .001) and very positive contexts (0.82 vs 0.05; OR = 0.35, 95% CI [0.21;0.59], p < .001). In sarcastic contexts, the opposite descriptive pattern is seen, with L1s rating it as more highly acceptable (1.20) than L2s (0.66). In very positive contexts, L2s find the ^_^ emoticon significantly more suitable (1.83) than L1s do (1.11) (OR = 0.38, 95% CI [0.22;0.65], p = .003). The same pattern is evident descriptively in general positive contexts (L2: 1.05 vs L1: 0.69). For both general negative and very negative contexts, there are no significant differences in suitability ratings between L1s and L2s. For sarcastic contexts, L1s find the :p emoticon significantly more suitable (1.47) than L2s do (0.79) (OR = 2.08, 95% CI [1.27;3.42], p = .025). In both general positive and very positive contexts, L1s and L2s do not differ in their ratings to this emoticon (ps > .8), with both groups rating its suitability for any type of positive context as neutral.

Paralleling the patterns observed in usage, L2s consistently find all kaomoji more suitable than L1s do: significantly so for ^_^ in very positive contexts, and descriptively so in general positive contexts, and for >_< and -_and ¬_¬ emoticons.

Meaning Equivalence

For each reference emoticon, participants only selected those options that they interpreted as having equivalent meaning to the given reference emoticon. Probabilities indicate the likelihood of rating an emoticon as having equivalent meaning to the reference emoticon.

Figure 8 shows the probabilities for each emoticon to be selected as equivalent to the corresponding reference emoticon by L1 and L2 participants. See Appendix Table A3 for full model outputs. For some emoticons, responses in both groups were concentrated at an extreme end of the probability scale, meaning they were judged as being non-equivalent to their reference emoticon so consistently that one or both groups produced very few positive equivalence responses (3 or fewer). These emoticons (n = 5) were excluded from inferential analysis due to insufficient response variation for meaningful comparison between groups; in such cases, only mean probabilities are reported. This left 23 emoticons in the inferential models.

For the :p emoticon, L1 participants were significantly less likely to rate the ;p emoticon as equivalent (0.23) than L2 participants were (0.39) (OR = 0.44, 95% CI [0.25;0.79], p = .023). Across all four reference emoticons, there were no other individual emoticons for which L1 and L2 users of English significantly differed in their equivalence ratings (all ps > .1).

Across these meaning equivalence responses, we observed a general tendency for emoticons that differ only by the addition of a nose element to receive high equivalence ratings, while alterations to the mouth element resulted in noticeably lower equivalence ratings. This pattern can be seen descriptively in Figure 8.

To explore this observed pattern further, we modelled how various elements and differences impact equivalence ratings. First, we coded each emoticon for the types of differences they featured relative to their reference emoticon. The categories were: differences in the nose element; differences in the mouth element; differences in the eyes element; mirroring of the emoticon; and, rotation of the emoticon. A few emoticons fell into multiple categories, such as a difference in both nose and mouth elements relative to the reference. Meanwhile, kaomoji are constructed so differently that individual differences cannot be separately identified. Emoticons variants that fell into multiple categories (n = 2) and kaomoji (n = 7) were excluded because any potential effects could not be attributed to any one feature. Only two variants involved more than one coded feature, and the possible feature combinations were not systematically represented, therefore interactions between variation types could not be reliably estimated. As such, the analysis considers the degree to which each type of difference individually effects emoticon meaning. Figure 9 summarises the probability of each difference category altering emoticon meaning. Each difference category significantly differed from all other difference categories (all Holmadjusted ps < .05). Differences to the nose element or rotating an emoticon had the lowest observed probabilities of impacting meaning (0.16 and 0.24 respectively), while mirroring, differences in the eyes element, and differences in the mouth element, had notably higher and progressively greater impact on meaning (0.49, 0.56, and 0.74). See Appendix Table A4 for full model outputs.

General Discussion

In this study, we examined how visual variation in emoticons impacts their use, contextual suitability, and perceived meaning equivalence across positive, negative, and sarcastic contexts, as well as the extent to which these patterns are shared by L1 and L2 users of English. Overall, results show the semantic impact of a variant depends not on the scale of the visual difference, but on the particular component or orientation that is altered.

Differences in the nose element and rotation had relatively little impact on perceived meaning, whereas mirroring and differences in the eyes and mouth had progressively greater effects. L1 and L2 participants showed a high degree of alignment across all three measures, with differences concentrated in particular emoticons, especially winking, tongue-out, and upright-oriented forms. However, contrary to our predictions, neither group had increased emoticon usage in sarcastic contexts relative to most other contexts. Together, these findings suggest emoticon meaning variation has a systematic connection to constituent components and visual features. L1 and L2 users of English largely share these connections, though some remain specific to particular language communities.

Factors Affecting Meaning

For the :) :( and :/ reference emoticons, each had three emoticon variants that were highly likely to be perceived as equivalent in meaning, with likelihoods over 0.74. The :p emoticon, however, had only one highly equivalent emoticon variant, with all others having meaning equivalence likelihoods below 0.51.

As noted above, we had broad predictions as to which elements might contribute to meaning, though the study was largely exploratory. In examining the perceived equivalence data, we observed general patterns whereby addition of a nose element had minimal impact on meaning, but altering mouth shape had far greater impact. Meanwhile, some orientational differences appeared to have a notable impact on meaning, while others did not. Through subsequent analysis, we explored the degree to which meaning was altered by differences in the nose, mouth, and eyes elements, and differences in rotation and mirroring orientations.

Overall, analysis revealed that minor visual variation can indeed impact perceived meaning, extending the findings of Fricke et al. (2024) from pictorial emoji to ASCII emoticons. Analysis also showed that the types of difference significantly differed from each other in the degree of they had impact on perceived meaning.

Elements

Our expectation that eyes and mouth elements would impact meaning more than nose elements was borne out and aligns with frequency data in prior literature (Thompson & Filik, 2016). However, it is notable that differences in the nose element do still impact perceived meaning, albeit to a vastly lower degree than both other elements. Also of note, differences in the mouth element resulted in by far the greatest deviation in perceived meaning relative to the corresponding reference emoticons. This may in part be influenced by the greater availability of options for the mouth element, which include curved parentheses, straight lines of varied angle, and several individual alpha-numeric characters, such as p or D or 0 (zero); whereas the eyes element is largely limited to colon or semicolon. So, while the eyes still provide significant information, the mouth is the most productive element in generating distinct meanings.

Despite its impact, keeping mouth shape the same does not force an emoticon to retain the same meaning, since other additions or changes to other elements (such as the eyes) can impact the meaning. However, making mouth shape different does have a very high likelihood of forcing a change in meaning. Overall, this indicates that the shape of the mouth element is of particular importance in the correct interpretation of an emoticon's meaning.

In terms of the eyes element, while comparison of individual forms is too fine-grained for the present study, we can nonetheless descriptively see that a change from : to = had rather less impact than a superficially smaller change from : to ; did. As such, it is not simply a change in shape that matters. Whether this is due to salience, frequency of exposure, or aptness in representing a target facial expression, is a factor that should be investigated further.

As expected the nose element had by far the lowest likelihood of altering perceived meaning, at just 0.16. However, in all observed cases, a change to the nose was via the addition of a nose relative to the reference emoticon. It could be argued that simply adding to an emoticon has less impact on meaning than altering an element. However, the only other instances of a purely additive change, which were the frowning brow in >:( and the tear in the :'( emoticon, greatly reduced perceived meaning similarity. This supports the idea that the nose is the least expressive or meaningful element within an emoticon, hence its overwhelming likelihood of being omitted in emoticon production (Thompson & Filik, 2016).

Orientation

Inverted versions of each reference emoticon typically had high meaning equivalence with their reference emoticon. That is, emoticons that are visually identical other than their orientation are interpreted as closely equivalent in meaning, including the :) and (: emoticons, the :( versus ): emoticons, and the :/ versus /: emoticons. However, the :p emoticon was far less likely to be seen as equivalent in meaning to the q: emoticon.

For both the :) and :( emoticons, the relationship to their inverted forms could be interpreted as either mirrored or rotated (i.e., mirroring or rotating 180 degrees would have the exact same visual result). For the :/ emoticon, which displays the same pattern of meaning equivalence, its inverted form of /: is clearly rotated relative to the reference, with the mouth always lowered under the right eye. Conversely, for the :p emoticon, which has notably less meaning equivalence with its q: inverted form, the nature of the inversion is clearly a mirroring. Modelling emoticon variants where the type of inversion is unambiguous (either clearly rotated or clearly mirrored) revealed that the probability of impacting meaning is only 0.24 for rotations, but 0.49 for mirrorings.

These various inversions result in emoticons with the top of the face to the right, rather than the default leftward orientation. Without a reference emoticon to compare them to, there would be no distinction between 'rotated' and 'mirrored'. Since we observe a difference in the effect on perceived meaning between rotated and mirrored, it is likely they are being processed as derivations of the reference emoticon. That being so, it would be interesting to explore why rotation has so much less impact than mirroring.

Taken together, the above suggests that when emoticons are encountered in a nondefault orientation, interpreting it as a mental rotation of the default is preferred over interpreting it as a mirroring. Prior research has shown a difference in both the legibility (Erlikhman et al., 2017) and the processing (Martinaud et al., 2016) of rotated versus mirrored text, typically showing that rotated text is considered easier than mirrored, with the present findings suggesting this extends beyond text to emoticons. At the same time, in neuroscientific literature, several studies have suggested emoticons are processed in similar ways to real human faces, such as in the identification of emotion (Yuasa et al., 2011), while others have shown either partial overlap or differences between emoticons and faces (see Aldunate & González-Ibáñez, 2017 for a review). The broader picture seems to be that emoticons are treated as somewhat like both faces and text, while not entirely being either.

Given the visually subtle yet meaningful distinctions in elements and orientation, in order to correctly process and interpret emoticons, we need to acquire a sensitivity to which visual variations are meaningful and which visual variations are not meaningful. This is comparable to other processes across cognitive and language development. In English, for example, we need to learn that the written difference between 'e' and 'o' results in the representation of different sounds, but variations to the letter 'e' in terms of different fonts, handwriting, cases, colours, and so on, do not impact the sound being represented.

L1 vs L2 Use and Interpretation

While individual emoticons are not restricted to any one language, their exact use and interpretation may vary across languages or cultures (Togans et al., 2021). This has likewise been observed for emoji (Wang et al., 2024). Nonetheless, emoticon use has been shown to increase in L2 contexts, potentially as a compensatory or supportive tool (Aragon et al., 2014; Vandergriff, 2014). For emoticons to be genuinely useful in these contexts, L1 and L2 users would need to be aligned in their usage and interpretations.

Our prediction was that L1 and L2 participants would pattern similarly, though the agreement might fall for frequent emoticons, and increased use might be exaggerated in sarcastic contexts. We did observe a very high degree of alignment between the two groups, but the level of agreement did not change with emoticon frequency. More surprisingly, reported likelihood of emoticon use actually fell for both groups in sarcastic contexts relative to most other contexts.

Agreement

Broadly speaking, participants with L1 English or L2 English were highly consistent with each other. The patterns of emoticon usage, judgements of contextual suitability, and interpretations of meaning equivalence all follow very similar overall distributions, with few individual emoticons revealing a significant difference between groups.

In each of the five context types, the emotions with the highest likelihood of use were the same for the two groups. This was clearest in the positive conditions, where the top two emoticons were noticeably more likely to be used than the remaining options. As well as usage, the emoticons most suited to each context were typically the same for the two groups, the pattern again being clearest in positive contexts. The least suitable emoticons for each context were more variable, though in most cases this did not constitute a significant group difference. Interpretations of meaning similarity between pairs of emoticons were also highly consistent between the language groups.

Overall, this indicates that in the majority of cases, L1 and L2 users of English use emoticons with the same frequency and interpret them in the same ways. As such, the usefulness of emoticons as markers of intent or clarification (Dresner & Herring, 2010; Filik et al., 2016; Skovholt et al., 2014) and as a compensatory or supportive tool in L2 contexts (Aragon et al., 2014; Vandergriff, 2014) is supported by the current findings.

Divergence

While there are clear, high level similarities between participants with L1 and L2 English, there are some notable points of divergence.

The ;) emoticon was rated by L2s as quite suitable for both general positive and very positive contexts, whereas L1s rated it as unsuited to the former and neutral in latter. While the smiling 'mouth' element appears positive, the winking eyes element appears to negate this interpretation for L1 English participants. In a complementary pattern, L1s rate this same emoticon as one of the most suited to a sarcastic context, while L2s rate it as one of the least suitable. Comparable differences have recently been reported for emoji, with winking emoji facilitating irony comprehension for US and UK participants, and smiling emoji being more effective for Chinese participants (Du, 2025; Du et al., 2026). This suggests associations between winking forms and ironic or sarcastic intent may be stronger in some languages or cultures than others. The current findings may reflect a related difference, although we did not distinguish between language and cultural background.

While the L1 and L2 groups rated the :p emoticon as having relatively neutral suitability for positive contexts, L1s were significantly more likely to use it themselves in a positive context. This suggests that native speakers of English see this emoticon as rather more positive than non-native speakers do. L1s also rated the same :p emoticon as significantly more suited to a sarcastic context than L2s did. Taken with the above, L1s appear to see a greater overlap between sarcasm and positivity than L2 participants. This could indicate that some of the meanings or uses of sarcasm are acquired earlier or are easier to access than others, hence L2 speakers tend to interpret sarcasm differently from L1 speakers. If so, the use of sarcasm for criticism (Adams, 2012) may be an aspect that is acquired earlier, while other more positive aspects, such as humour or playfulness (Roberts & Kreuz, 1994) or softening the impact of a message (Dews & Winner, 1995; Harris & Pexman, 2003) come later. This connects with the earlier discussion of the ;) emoticon: if playfulness is seen as an aspect of sarcasm by L1s but not by L2s, this would explain why the playful wink element is interpreted by L1s as a marker of sarcasm.

A broader pattern of divergence involves the upright-oriented kaomoji. Across all context types, L2 participants were consistently more likely to use kaomoji than L1s, and also gave them consistently higher suitability ratings, though these patterns were not always statistically significant. This broadly lines up with previous research on preferences for leftrotated emoticons versus kaomoji (Park et al., 2014), though the present findings cannot be attributed specifically to factors such as culture or language script.

Conclusion

Our findings reveal how certain types of visual variation within emoticons influence their meaning interpretation, while others do not. This is not a factor that is easily measured by the scale of visual difference: some visually obvious changes, such as the addition of a nose element, have minimal effect on meaning; other visually minor changes, such as from colon to semicolon for the eyes, drastically impact perceived meaning. The lowest impact comes from the nose element and from rotating an emoticon, while the greatest impact is produced by the eyes and mouth elements, as well as mirroring an emoticon. The lower impact of rotation versus mirroring is comparable with established processing preferences in textual reading. Understanding the ways different emoticon elements interact with meaning should be useful for translation software, sentiment analysis, natural language processing, and language teaching, especially in terms of digital literacy. The current findings should, however, be expanded with further studies that include additional context types and a wider range of emoticon variations.

We also saw that native and non-native users of English pattern very closely in their overarching usage and meaning interpretation. It has previously been established that emoticons are efficient markers of intention. From the present study, we see this holds true in a second language, suggesting emoticons are a valid tool for facilitating conversations in cross-cultural and cross-linguistic contexts. Importantly, there are exceptions to this, primarily for more subtle variations in emoticons and contexts. While emoticons are considered non-linguistic and independent of any single language, they are still conventionalised within given language communities. Their precise usage within a particular language context needs to be acquired alongside the rest of that language. In a highly digital age, this is an important consideration for language learning and digital literacy. While our study included a large sample of non-native speakers, further studies that focus on particular languages and cultures would be required to determine whether the observed effects are modulated by language-specific factors, such as the script of the L1 (logographic, abugida, abjad), or cultural factors, such as attitudes towards humour or emotional expression.

The present findings have several limitations to bear in mind. Although participants were asked to judge broad context types rather than individual messages, the illustrative example that was provided for each context type may have influenced how that context was interpreted. Since the investigation of variation was exploratory, the current study used frequently occurring emoticon variants identified in previous research, rather than systematically manipulating each possible visual feature. Future studies could systematically manipulate nose, eyes, mouth, rotation, and mirroring, as well as other features, and could examine the possible additive effects of emoticons that contain multiple variations. Although all emoticons included in the current study were identified as frequently occuring in production, this does not necessarily rule out influences from item-level familiarity or related traits; controlling for such factors in future work will require extensive norming, and ideally per-participant ratings. Further research could explore the impact of participant variables, such as how L2 participants differ in terms of English proficiency, first language, writing system, and cultural background, and how L1 participants differ in aspects such as knowledge of other languages.
